newsitem.title: USA: FOMC meeting -- What the Fed is looking at.
newsitem.headline: FOMC meeting -- What the Fed is looking at.

text.p: The Federal Open Market Committee is meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday to set interest rates against a backdrop of tight labor markets and steady inflation as the U.S. economy heads for a seventh straight year of expansion.
-- MARKET EXPECTATIONS

The latest Reuters poll showed only one out of 26 economists -- Ken Bercuson, head of research at SBC Warburg -- calling for a 25-basis-point hike this week in the funds rate, at 5.25 percent since January 1996.
The main reason cited for forecasting steady Fed policy is the absence of existing inflationary pressure.

But 16 of the 26 economists polled foresaw a tightening in 1997, with six predicting the first hike at the March 27 FOMC meeting. They expected the first move to be by 25 points. Only the Conference Board predicted a 50-point hike in March.
Most often cited for tightening expectations were above-trend growth and tight labor markets.
Not included in the latest Reuters poll was Joseph Carson, managing director at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, who is expecting a 25-point funds rate hike on Wednesday.
Both Carson and Bercuson cited signs of incipient wage-led inflation as well as hints of a tightening in Fed chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony before the Senate on January 21.
MRF Inc advisor and former Fed Board Director Stephen Axilrod expected the Fed to vote for a tightening bias and move at the first sign of rising wage-related inflation.
-- GREENSPAN'S RECENT COMMENTS
CURRENT OUTLOOK: "The economy has retained considerable vigor, with few signs of the imbalances and inflationary tensions that have disrupted past expansions."
PREEMPTIVE POLICY: "It is not the conditions prevailing today that are critical but rather those likely to prevail six to 12 months, or even longer, from now."
WAGE/INFLATION: "The relatively modest wage gains we've seen are a transitional rather than a lasting phenomenon."
WAGE PRESSURE: "The recent pickup in some measure of wages suggests the transition may already be running its course."

KEY POLICY ISSUE: "The important question from a monetary policy point of view is whether prospective labor market conditions will be consistent with the maintenance of satisfactory price performance."
OVERSTATEMENT OF INFLATION: "It does not alter the relationship between resource utilization and inflation."
RISING DOLLAR: "Almost never" the determining factor in U.S. monetary policy.

STOCK MARKET: "How do we know when irrationale exuberance has unduly escalated asset values... Evaluating shifts in... asset prices particularly must be an integral part of the development of monetary policy." Later, Greenspan said the comment "was not a shot from the hip."
-- FOMC MINUTES
-- A tighening bias was in place from July to November. The minutes of the December meeting are released on Friday.
-- Minneapolis Fed President Gary Stern dissented for a tightening at three FOMC meetings between July and November.
-- The FOMC described at its January 30-31, 1996 meeting the real funds rate as "still a bit to the firm side," before lowering the then 5.50-percent funds rate by 25 basis points.

-- The FOMC called the "real funds rate... probably not greatly out of line with its appropriate level" at the May meeting when the benchmark rate was at 5.25 percent. The jobless rate slipped and the ECI's wage component rose since.

-- The FOMC concluded in November abandoning a bias toward tightening "might signal, inaccuraetly, the Federal Reserve was less concerned about the possibility of a modest upward trajectory in price inflation."
-- FED RECENT COMMENTS

-- Atlanta Fed President Jack Guynn outlined policy choices, saying "If we want to maintain the current rate of inflation, then the Fed's current stance is probably appropriate under current conditions... If we want to make further progress on inflation, then we need to be looking for opportunities over time to nudge the rate still lower."
-- Gov. Lawrence Meyer warned "I have a slightly greater concern that inflation will increase than that the economy will lapse into persistent, below-trend growth and face rising unemployment."
-- San Francisco Fed Robert Parry said "The trend rate of growth is about 2.0 percent... If it's significantly faster than that, I think I would be concerned."
-- Kansas City Fed Thomas Hoenig concurred "We think the growth rate is 2.0- to 2.5 percent and that can be sustained without incurring inflation, and if you get above that, you threaten inflation."
